The uilleann pipes are Ireland's national bagpipe, an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.122.2+422.221.1. The bag is filled by a small bellows strapped between the waist and the right arm, and the other elbow squeezes the bag to control the airflow; the air goes to the chanter, the drones and the regulators. The chanter is stopped with the fingers, can overblow two octaves, and is usually held on the thigh with its end closed; the three drones sound continuously an octave apart, and the three regulators are keyed with the wrist or the hand and can play simple chords. Playing is mostly indoors and almost always seated; early on the instrument was common among Protestant Anglo-Irish communities and gentleman pipers, and clergy also used it in place of the organ.
愛爾蘭風笛為氣鳴樂器，源自愛爾蘭。演奏時幾乎總採坐姿，風箱綁於腰部與右臂，以另一: The uilleann pipes are an aerophone from Ireland. They are played almost always seated: the bellows are strapped between the waist and the right arm, the other elbow squeezes the bag, and that squeeze controls the air going to the reeds; the chanter is usually held on the thigh, stopped with the fingers, and overblown to reach the upper octave. The wrist can open the keys of the regulators to accompany with simple chords. Because the instrument is complex, a beginner usually starts on a practice set with only the chanter.
愛爾蘭風笛（Uilleann pipes）為愛爾蘭民族風笛。現名20世紀前無記錄: The uilleann pipes are Ireland's national bagpipe. The present name is not recorded before the twentieth century and was coined by Grattan Flood; the older name Union pipes is found at the end of the eighteenth century, and a poem of 1796 already uses it. The early Irish bagpipe was close to the Scottish Highland bagpipe and later declined. At the beginning of the eighteenth century the bellows-blown Union or Uilleann pipes appeared, developing at the same time as the Northumbrian smallpipes and the Scottish Lowland bagpipe. A tutor by Geoghegan in the 1740s calls the early form the Pastoral or New bagpipe, which could be played sitting or standing, and it later spread to Ireland, Scotland and England. The earliest surviving instruments belong to the second half of the eighteenth century. Early on it was mostly used by Protestant Anglo-Irish communities and by clergy. At the end of the nineteenth century the Taylor brothers promoted the D pitch, replacing the flat sets that were mostly in D-flat, C, B and B-flat.
